title: Slipstream: nonlinear beam dynamics in PyTorch
summary: Slipstream is a PyTorch package for nonlinear beam dynamics in storage rings, linacs and photoinjectors. It provides CPU and GPU particle tracking, field-map injector models with space charge, and automatic differentiation along supported tracking paths. Comparisons with elegant, ASTRA, GPT and other codes assess accuracy and computational cost for nonlinear ring tracking, optics matching and photoinjectors. Ring tunes agree with elegant to $10^{-9}$. For the tested ring workloads with tens of thousands of particles, GPU tracking in float32 is hundreds of times faster than the single-threaded CPU implementations compared here. Automatic differentiation reduces the time for 24-parameter optics matching by an order of magnitude compared to finite differences. Using a high-brightness photo-injector as an example, final horizontal emittances agree with ASTRA to about 1% at 20 and 100pC and differ by $\approx$4% at 250pC. For $2^{18}$ macroparticles, Slipstream's faster default settings take 14s on an RTX 3050 GPU and give emittances within 2% of that of ASTRA. Additional tests examine coherent synchrotron radiation, dynamic aperture and resistive-wall impedance. The package was developed predominantly by AI coding assistants under human direction. These comparisons identify where its models, GPU execution and derivatives are useful for repeated simulations in scans, fits and optimisation.

title: Toward light-controlled transverse Wigner ordering in attosecond electron beams
comment: 25 pages (13 pages main text including 3 figures, plus 12 pages Supplemental Material)
summary: Kinetic fluctuations and space-charge expansion hinder Wigner ordering in free-electron beams. Here we propose a laser-driven route toward transient, substrate-free Wigner ordering that combines photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) attosecond bunching, synchronized magnetic focusing, and spatial preconditioning. Classical relaxation and zero-temperature fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo trap benchmarks show that sixfold order survives quantum fluctuations from 1 T to sub-Tesla fields, defining ultrafast preparation targets.

title: Electron versus positron impact ionization of inner shells of heavy atoms: distortion, exchange and relativistic effects
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures; numerical data in ancillary file
summary: Triple differential cross sections are presented for electron and positron impact ionization of the K shells of Cu, Ag, Au and U and the L shells of Ag. Relativistic effects are important throughout. For positrons the recoil maximum is suppressed and the recoil-region spin asymmetry changes sign; for the $2s$ shell the binary peak changes. In symmetric geometry, where theory reproduces the measured absolute electron cross section, the positron peak lies on the other side of zero recoil. Measurements would test relativistic ionization theory in a regime that electron experiments cannot reach.

title: Probing the Rung-Mott Insulator in Bosonic Two-Leg Ladders
summary: Mott insulators typically appear at integer densities, but certain lattice geometries or non-local interactions can stabilise Mott insulators at fractional densities. In this work, we study strongly interacting two-leg ladders using ultracold bosonic atoms around half-filling, and identify the rung-Mott insulating (RMI) phase through its characteristic rung occupation in site-resolved measurements. We probe its excitation spectrum via lattice modulation spectroscopy, and interpret the observed spectra using numerical simulations that include the driven dynamics, coupling to multiple excited states, and energy offsets. As with other Mott insulators, the RMI phase is characterized through its incompressibility, which we probe via a site-resolved analysis of densities and chemical potentials. Our results provide direct insight into the excitation dynamics of a strongly correlated ladder system, and pave the way for studying transport and further dynamical properties in low-dimensional quantum systems with programmable lattice geometries.

title: Perturbation of CO A1Π by a3Π should have been undetectable: detection, mechanism, and surprises
summary: A direct perturbation between the $a^3Π$ and $A^1Π$ vibrational levels of two electronic states that belong to the same electronic configuration of the carbon monoxide molecule should be unobservably weak because the vibrational overlap integral $\langle a^3Π,v' \mid A^1Π,v'' \rangle$ for their near-degenerate levels is extremely small. Yet level-shift and transition-intensity signatures of the $a^3Π(v = 13) \sim A^1Π(v = 2)$ perturbation are unmistakably present in the $^{13}\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O}$ isotopologue. A detailed study of, among others, the $A^1Π$ - $X^1Σ^+(2, 0)$, $B^1Σ^+$ - $A^1Π(0, 2)$, and $C^1Σ^+$ - $A^1Π(0, 2)$ spectra, obtained by the VUV- and Vis-FT complementary techniques in the energy regions of the six crossing points ($e$- and $f$-symmetry, $|Ω| = 0, 1, 2$) between the $a^3Π(v = 13)$ and $A^1Π(v = 2)$ states, reveal that the perturbation pathways are indirect, primarily facilitated by the $e^3Σ^-(v = 4)$ state, and that quantum mechanical interferences via its F1e and F3e components occur.

title: Symmetry-constrained order hierarchy of connected optical responses in a five-level Rydberg-EIT medium
summary: Determining the connected many-body correlations required for a nonlinear optical response of a given order is a central challenge in interacting open quantum systems. We establish a symmetrybased selection rule for connected optical responses in a driven-dissipative Rydberg-EIT model. Under the specified Lindblad conditions, local phase covariance and zero-probe factorization imply that an n-atom connected contribution to the root optical coherence is forbidden below probe-amplitude order 2n-1. Consequently, optical-response coefficients through fifth order involve at most three-atom connected clusters, without assuming weak interatomic interactions. Direct finite-cluster calculations confirm the predicted lowest allowed orders, while an illustrative Maxwell-propagation calculation shows that triplet contributions can partially oppose pair-induced polarization rotation. Our results establish a rigorous connection between optical perturbation order and the connected many-body sectors that can contribute to it.

title: First-principles phase diagram of monolayer CrS$_2$ polymorphs under biaxial strain and its sensitivity to the Hubbard U parameter
summary: In correlated two-dimensional magnets the balance between competing electronic and magnetic phases is often set by the strength of the on-site Coulomb interaction, so that the predicted ground state can hinge on a parameter that is not uniquely defined. Monolayer CrS$_2$ lies squarely in this regime, hosting several energetically close polymorphs whose character ranges from non-magnetic semiconducting to magnetically ordered metallic. We therefore investigate, using DFT$+U$ within the generalized gradient approximation, the structural, magnetic, and electronic properties of the 1H, 1T, 1T$'$, and 1T$''$ polymorphs of monolayer CrS$_2$ under varying Hubbard interactions ($U=0$--$8$~eV) and biaxial strain ($-10\%$ to $+10\%$). The 1T-derived structures remain metallic and magnetic throughout, with $U$ acting mainly as a spectral renormalization. The 1H phase behaves differently, passing from a non-magnetic semiconductor through an antiferromagnetic semiconducting regime before metallizing, so that the gap closes as $U$ increases while the local Cr moment grows monotonically. Biaxial tensile strain at fixed $U$ induces a similar sequence of transitions. Along both tuning pathways, the two inequivalent nearest-neighbor Cr--Cr exchange channels progressively separate and cross, with the parallel-spin channel becoming dominant, accompanied by a breathing-type bond disproportionation. Independent calculations with a localized-orbital implementation reproduce the overall evolution but yield shifted critical values of $U$ and of strain, demonstrating the robustness of the phase diagram while highlighting the implementation dependence of the transition thresholds.

title: Efficient spin-lattice dynamics and spin thermometry with machine-learned magnetic potentials
summary: In finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics, conventional force-only spin thermometers fail for energies nonlinear in each spin, while the standard semi-implicit SIB integrator requires two model evaluations per step. Here we introduce a geometric-probe spin temperature that is exact for arbitrary high-order smooth Hamiltonians using first-order spin forces alone without Hessians, making it naturally suited for nonlinear many-body machine-learning (ML) magnetic potentials. Complementarily, our cached-field integrator (CFI) stays second-order accurate with a single model evaluation per step, about halving the time per step with ML potentials. Extensive benchmarks against Monte Carlo across analytic and ML systems confirm both exact thermometry and accurate thermodynamics.

title: Variance and Higher-Order Moments in Computational Fluctuating Hydrodynamics with Multiplicative Noise
summary: Fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHD) models mesoscopic fluid systems by augmenting classical conservation laws with stochastic flux terms governed by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. While traditional validation of computational FHD (CFHD) algorithms focuses primarily on second-order central moments of equilibrium fluctuations, accurately resolving higher-order moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, is essential for evaluating non-linear functions of hydrodynamic fields. In this work, we analyze finite-volume CFHD discretizations to evaluate second-, third-, and fourth-order central moments of thermodynamic fluctuations. Using the one-dimensional stochastic heat equation, we demonstrate that incorporating multiplicative noise is necessary to recover the expected gamma distribution for temperature in the canonical ensemble, whereas additive noise models yield a Gaussian distribution that fails to capture non-zero skewness and excess kurtosis. We also derive analytical expressions for inherent modeling errors that persist in the limit of vanishing time step for a variety of boundary conditions. Furthermore, we introduce an improved formulation for Dirichlet boundary conditions that eliminates large boundary-adjacent errors in the third central moment present in traditional boundary treatments. We also examine higher-order temporal integration schemes, demonstrating that Stratonovich-based integrators, such as Heun's predictor-corrector method, can reduce these modeling errors. Finally, numerical simulations of the full compressible, stochastic Navier--Stokes equations confirm the generality and practical applicability of the findings obtained from the stochastic heat equation.

title: Modeling of Chemically Reactive Gas Flows for Multi-Scale Problems
summary: Accurate modeling of chemical reactions plays a key role in the investigation of high-temperature flows. The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method provides highly accurate solutions for such flows. However, its computational cost becomes prohibitive for low Knudsen regimes. Particle-based continuum methods employing the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) or Fokker-Planck approximations have gained increasing attention in recent years, improve computational efficiency in low-Knudsen regimes by modeling relaxation processes rather than binary collisions, while retaining the particle approach that enables straightforward coupling with DSMC. In the last years, different continuum-based models in the open-source particle code PICLas have been extended to simulate gas mixtures with internal energy modes. The present work focuses on modeling of chemically reactive gas mixtures in the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK model. Model accuracy is assessed for two test cases of a reactive gases confined in a reservoir.

title: Parametric neural-network wavefunctions across a bosonic phase transition
summary: We propose Boseformer, a universal attention-based neural-network architecture for representing the wavefunctions of particles with bosonic quantum statistics, including superfluid and crystal phases. The model is trained to generate the wavefunction as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter across the quantum phase transition between these phases. Once trained with variational Monte Carlo optimization, it can serve as a foundation model describing the phase transition without the need to retrain it for individual parameter values. We demonstrate our method on a system of two-dimensional bosons with $1/r^3$ repulsive interaction.

title: From Fermions to Vortices: Microscopic Simulations of Phase Ordering in a d-Wave Superconductor
summary: Describing bath-induced superconducting phase ordering directly from a microscopic fermionic Hamiltonian remains a formidable challenge. Here we develop a microscopic framework for this problem using the recently introduced adiabatic variational principle (AVP) and demonstrate its application to a two-dimensional $d$-wave superconductor. The central construction maps evolving, spatially inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, with the associated Lagrange multipliers determining the thermodynamic driving forces. This enables dissipative evolution of the superconducting order while retaining its microscopic electronic structure, without assuming a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functional. Starting from disordered pairing configurations, we resolve the emergence of phase coherence through vortex-antivortex annihilation and the accompanying evolution of local electronic spectra. Vortex decay and dynamical scaling recover the characteristic kinetics of two-dimensional phase ordering, providing a nontrivial benchmark of the framework. The solver-independent AVP formulation opens a route to microscopic studies of dissipative ordering and metastability in superconductors with intertwined stripe and pair-density-wave orders.

title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures; Supplementary Information (15 pages) included
summary: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.

title: Packing the Bragg sphere: complete three-dimensional photonic band gaps at the refractive index of polymers (1.55)
summary: Complete 3D photonic band gaps have so far been found only at refractive-index contrasts of about 1.9 and above, reached by rod-connected diamond lattice structures. Reciprocal-space design of quasiperiodic structures recently achieved considerable emission attenuation at much lower contrasts [L. Maiwald et al., Adv. Optical Mater. 10, 2100785 (2022)]. Here we implement systematic search and reciprocal-space design of periodic 3D structures with complete band gaps, solving a discrete optimization problem on an integer lattice. A gap above a high band needs the strongest Fourier components of the dielectric close to the Bragg sphere of that band. Crystals with large cells, started from Fourier peaks at the vertices of a polyhedron on this sphere and optimized against densely refined band edges, open complete gaps down to an index contrast of 1.55, that of common polymers against air. A rational approximant of an icosidodecahedron gave the most efficient location of the Fourier peaks among the polyhedra tested. Numerical calculations confirm the gaps over a resolution series, with band edges searched over the whole Brillouin zone. The best designs are connected porous networks, suited to a microwave test with printed polymer. A rigorous bound, valid for any structure, does not exclude gaps at lower index, and the next rational approximants of the icosidodecahedron, whose Bragg zones match bands 576 and 2440 almost exactly, point to where gaps at even lower contrast may be sought.

title: Mixing and Preserving Properties of Non-van der Waals 2D Materials in Sandwich-like Heterostructures
summary: Heterostructure interfaces created by stacking two-dimensional (2D) materials outline an appealing route towards achieving advanced electronic and magnetic functionalities at the nanoscale. Non-van der Waals (non-vdW) sandwich-like heterostructures (HSs) are build out of non-vdW 2D materials derived from non-layered crystals and establish a new frontier enabling strong interfacial coupling. Employing ab initio density functional theory (DFT), we investigate two classes of such trilayer HSs: purely non-vdW assemblies and hybrid vdW/non-vdW/vdW stacks. We show that non-vdW sandwiches undergo pronounced geometric reconstruction forming chemically bonded interfaces with large absolute binding energies up to an order of magnitude larger than those of conventional vdW HSs. These strong interactions drive extensive electronic hybridization, band gap renormalization, and tunable interlayer magnetic coupling. In contrast, vdW encapsulation largely protects the intrinsic atomic and electronic structure of the non-vdW sheet from the environment , while enabling charge transfer doping of the vdW layers. Our results thus establish sandwich HSs a versatile interface design platform, spanning interaction regimes from weakly perturbed encapsulation to strongly interacting chemically bonded systems with emergent electronic and magnetic behavior.

title: Thermodynamics of complex crystals from a generalized mean-field bond model
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Code: https://github.com/raynol-dsouza/mean-field-bond-model (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24493341). Data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24466123
summary: We extend our previously introduced mean-field bond model from unary fcc lattices to crystals with multiple chemical species and sublattices, accurately predicting finite-temperature thermodynamics without statistical sampling. Our generalization reformulates the model in terms of the Wyckoff positions of the crystal, representing each by one atom, and solving for the bond density of the reference bond of each of its neighbor shells. Bond-bond correlation functions are built from the zero-temperature force constants, allowing the deviation of every bond in the crystal to be expressed through linear functions of the reference bond of a shell. Thermodynamic self-consistency is enforced by requiring a single virial temperature for the whole crystal, and compatibility of average bond lengths with crystal volume. Model predictions are validated against molecular dynamics simulations of unary, binary, and ternary crystals using Morse-type bonding potentials, parametrized for each shell from the force constants of empirical interatomic potentials at several isotropic strains. In each case, the predicted bond densities and thermodynamics agree with the simulations to within their statistical uncertainty. We discuss strategies for combining the model with bonding potentials parametrized from first principles and foundation models to predict the finite-temperature thermodynamics of complex crystals at ab initio accuracy without statistical sampling.

title: Augmented Imaginary-Time Evolution of Neural Quantum States with Implicit Time Steps
summary: Finding the ground states of quantum many-body systems remains a central challenge in physics and quantum chemistry. Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) offers a natural, widely used route, but its convergence is typically asymptotic. Variational approaches restrict this evolution to parameterized manifolds, with neural quantum states (NQS) providing flexible representations commonly optimized via stochastic reconfiguration (SR). Their performance depends on the geometry of the variational manifold, the convergence properties of ITE, and the stability of finite-step explicit (forward) integrators. By exploiting local geometric information of the energy landscape, the recently introduced augmented imaginary-time evolution (AITE) can, in principle, reach the ground state in finite imaginary time. To exploit the accelerated convergence of AITE in NQS optimization, we first combine an implicit Euler step with Galerkin projection to derive an implicit SR scheme that permits large, stable steps and substantially outperforms conventional methods. We use it to formulate an implicit version of AITE and show that its acceleration persists under variational projection and finite-step integration with asymptotically quadratic convergence of the energy error. With finite sampling, implicit schemes yield consistent gains, and implicit AITE becomes increasingly advantageous.

title: OMNI-P3x universal neural network potential for large-scale computational photochemistry workflows
summary: Computational photochemistry supports the design and understanding of new materials. However, the high cost of excited-state quantum-mechanical (QM) calculations makes screening large molecular libraries prohibitively expensive. To address this limitation, we introduce OMNI-P3x, a universal machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) for singlet ground- and excited-state simulations of neutral and charged organic molecules. Trained on both ground- and excited-state conformations, it performs complete computational photochemistry workflows with accuracy approaching TD-DFT. We demonstrate its practical applicability by screening a combinatorial library of 234,375 flavylium derivatives, where the pretrained model performs ground-state geometry optimization and predicts absorption properties without additional QM calculations. Following fine-tuning, we further screen 162,960 xanthene-based dyes, identifying new candidates for red, near-infrared and short-wavelength infrared emission. Furthermore, state-dependent neural charges, learned without reference atomic charges, provide an interpretable picture of intramolecular charge redistribution upon excitation.

title: SPARK: Spectral Preconditioned Analytic Residual Kolmogorov Arnold Networks for incompressible Navier Stokes equations
comment: 68 pages, 16 figures, 12 tables, to be submitted to Journal of Computational Physics
summary: We propose Spectral Jet KAN (SJ-KAN) to reduce the cost of differentiation and the network complexity of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for the Navier-Stokes (NS) equations. The input coordinates are embedded through Chebyshev bases whose spatial derivatives are known in closed form, and all differentiation matrices are computed once for the collocation points before training. A single linear layer compresses the Chebyshev bases into a few latent features, and a single nonlinear Chebyshev Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (CKAN) layer maps these features to the physical variables. Because the basis derivatives are known in advance and the compression is linear, the spatial derivatives in the NS equations are carried through the network analytically by a fixed sequence of matrix products and elementwise operations. Automatic differentiation (AD) is used only in backpropagation, to compute the gradients of the loss with respect to the network weights. We examine three variants of SJ-KAN (JetKAN, JetKAN-F, JetKAN-H), which differ in how the output layer maps the latent features to the physical variables. All variants are tested on the Taylor-Green vortex and on the lid driven cavity at Reynolds numbers Re = 100, 1000, 5000 and 10,000. The results are compared with a KAN that uses AD (PIKAN) and with a standard PINN. The SJ-KAN variants reach comparable or better accuracy than both, with up to 47 times fewer parameters and up to 8.2 times faster training per epoch. SJ-KAN also solves the lid driven cavity flow at Re = 10,000 without any reference data and with fewer than 9,000 trainable parameters. These results show that analytic derivative propagation, a small spectral input layer and a single KAN layer give a faster and simpler solver than methods based on AD, also for flows at high Reynolds numbers.

title: Parton Physics in the Schwinger Model from Matrix Product States
summary: Parton distribution functions (PDFs) and light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) encode the non-perturbative structure of hadrons in terms of their partonic constituents. They are defined through matrix elements containing parton operators that are connected by a Wilson line along a light-front direction, which makes them difficult to access in Euclidean lattice calculations. We demonstrate how parton functions can be directly obtained in Minkowski space using the Hamiltonian framework. We compute fermion and antifermion PDFs, LCDAs, and decay constants of the vector meson in the Schwinger model for several fermion masses. States in Hilbert space are efficiently represented by tensor networks, with an expressivity that is systematically controlled by a bond dimension. The light-front Wilson line is implemented as a stepwise evolution on the lattice that alternates spatial shifts of an external charge with Trotterized time-evolution steps acting on a matrix product state. All systematic uncertainties are quantified by varying and extrapolating in the lattice spacing, volume, bond dimension, gauge-field truncation, and Trotter step width. The slow growth of the entanglement entropy makes moderate bond dimensions sufficient, which supports the feasibility of using tensor networks for computing light-front matrix elements in more general settings. We confirm that the computed distributions fulfill the expected normalizations, momentum sum rules, and symmetry properties.

title: Neural-operator acceleration of bidirectional phonon Boltzmann-Fourier coupling for multiscale heat transport in silicon fin arrays
summary: Localized heating in semiconductor devices can produce non-diffusive phonon transport near heat-generating regions, while heat spreading through the surrounding substrate remains well described by Fourier conduction. We present a hybrid framework that couples a pretrained neural operator for the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) within individual fins to a Fourier model of a shared substrate. To reduce the cost of repeated BTE solves across fin positions and coupling iterations, a DeepONet maps each fin's substrate-interface temperature and heating state to its temperature and heat-flux fields. The operator is trained on interface temperatures generated by a linearized proxy of the coupled problem, which avoids explicit training data collection from full coupled runs. An energy-balance penalty regularizes the learned operator, and a mixed finite-element formulation represents substrate heat flux in an H(div)-conforming space. The two models exchange temperature and normal heat flux through a non-overlapping Schwarz iteration with adaptive Aitken relaxation. We evaluate the framework on an idealized three-dimensional array of 100 silicon fins. For a held-out switching configuration, the neural-operator-Fourier solution differs from the direct BTE-Fourier reference by a maximum of 0.3 K in temperature and 0.6% in relative flux across all fins. Excluding the one-time substrate factorization, the coupled surrogate run takes about 50 s, compared with 2 h 28 min for direct coupling, a speedup of approximately 180x. Additional held-out switching patterns converge with the same trained operator. These results demonstrate neural-operator acceleration of bidirectional kinetic-continuum coupling for the tested geometry and material. This bidirectional strategy may extend to other multiscale materials problems coupling learned local neural models with continuum solvers.

title: Nonlinear non-modal stability and minimal perturbations in electroconvection driven by unipolar injection
comment: 41 pages, 16 figures. Supplementary code in the ancillary files. The following article has been submitted to Physics of Fluids. After it is published, it will be found at https://pubs.aip.org/aip/pof
summary: Electroconvection in a dielectric liquid subjected to unipolar charge injection is subcritical. Convection can be sustained well below the threshold of linear stability theory, and experiments report onset far below it. We use nonlinear non-modal optimization to determine the smallest charge perturbations that trigger convection below the linear threshold. The method, based on a direct--adjoint formulation of the full electrohydrodynamic equations, recovers the classical linear threshold in the limit of small amplitudes. At finite amplitude, the most dangerous perturbations are localized charge deficits rather than excesses, because a deficit relaxes more slowly under Coulomb repulsion. The minimal perturbation needed for transition grows from about 0.5% of the injected charge near the linear threshold to 3% at two thirds of it, where the convective branch ends, in agreement with direct numerical simulations. Near the critical amplitude, trajectories approach an unstable steady state, the edge state, that separates the basins of attraction of rest and convection and originates from the critical linear mode. The damped oscillatory modes involved in the growth of the optimal perturbations are transit-time modes of the ion drift. The convective mode is the first of them, made stationary by the coupling with the flow, which explains why the instability sets in as a steady motion. Small charge fluctuations can therefore lower the onset of electroconvection to about two thirds of the linear threshold, helping to explain the discrepancy between linear theory and experiments.

title: Effect of humidity and phase transition on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows
summary: We investigate the effect of humidity on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows taking into account the effect of phase transitions on turbulent transport. We find that the coefficients of turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour decrease with increase the turbulent Damköhler number (the ratio of turbulent time in the integral scale and phase transition time for condensation of water vapour), while the coefficients of the mutual turbulent diffusion that describe the turbulent cross effects increase with this parameter. For large turbulent Damköhler number, the coefficient of turbulent diffusion of droplets is strongly depleted when the evaporation of droplets is much faster than the condensation of water vapour. The obtained theoretical relationships are potentially useful in modelling applications in the atmospheric turbulence.

title: Emergent cloud patterns from stochastic jump models of parcel microphysics
summary: Warm clouds organize into bands, cells, and intricate wave networks, yet the dynamical mechanisms connecting these forms remain difficult to isolate. To bridge unresolved parcel microphysics and cloud organization, we formulate a spatial jump-process model of cloud-water and rain-water anomalies in an activated regime and analyze its mean-field closure. Eliminating fast supersaturation adjustment from droplet growth and vapor transport supplies a screened environmental kernel, which we couple to a cubic Stuart-Landau oscillatory law. Averaging over Poisson parcel episodes and closing third-order moments yields a pseudoparabolic Ginzburg--Landau equation (PGLE), whose mixed space--time derivative encodes dynamic inertia, slowing fine-scale relaxation. Unlike diffusive amplitude equations, the PGLE splits into a regularized nonlinear Schrödinger Hamiltonian sector and a pseudoparabolic Allen--Cahn gradient sector governed by a conserved Noether charge, alongside an open-system liquid-water budget separating conversion from vapor exchange, fallout, and triad-driven domain-mean oscillations. Exact stability criteria show how dynamic inertia and amplitude-dependent frequency shifts (twist) control modulational loss of synchrony and resonant cross-carrier sideband gain above a critical twist threshold. Numerical integrations show that increasing twist transforms undulatus-like bands into defect-rich asperitas-like waves via defect proliferation, while subcritical competition consolidates cellular patterns into rolls. Even without twist, random anomalies evolve into a persistent cellular exclusion scale and actinoform-like spiral arms, while 1D wave breakup reorganizes into a two-frequency combination-tone spectrum. The jump model identifies omitted fluctuation moments for calibration against large-eddy simulations.

title: A consistent generalised kinetic equation for damped ocean waves
summary: Contemporary spectral wave models, including those used in operational wave forecasts and in coupled earth system models, assume damping and non-linear wave energy exchange to be independent. Here, we critically examine this assumption. Starting from the equations of weakly non-linear waves, we rigorously derive a governing equation that consistently couples damping and non-linear interactions. This consistent generalised kinetic equation does not lead to an appreciable change in total wave--energy dissipation, but compared to the standard additive damping approach there is a noticeable difference in the distribution of energy among the wave frequencies. This effect is particularly important for weak damping, and is a consequence of a memory effect retained in model. Even stronger differences are observed when damping is allowed to depend on wave frequency, as is characteristic of many wave processes of growing interest such as the interaction with other components of the earth system, e.g. the cryosphere. Compared to the purely additive formulation, our new damped generalised kinetic equation has improved numerical stability characteristics. The formulation presented therefore provides a possible basis for future operational wave modelling. While our results are for ocean waves, the derived generalised kinetic equation can be applied to other weakly nonlinear dispersive systems where external damping (or forcing) applies.

title: Elastic rebound in viscous fluid: an efficient rigid--elastic splitting with an asymptotic gap model
summary:
We formulate and test a model for an elastic body that falls under gravity onto the bottom of a container filled with a viscous incompressible fluid and rebounds without topological contact. The body is a rigid body plus a small, quasi-static elastic deformation, represented by a fixed compliance operator. In the near-contact patch, the thin fluid film is described by a Reynolds equation with cavitation. This allows the use of coarse meshes that need not resolve the gap, enabling efficient simulation. The film is coupled implicitly to the elastic surface displacement and to the rigid normal motion. The bulk fluid is coupled monolithically to the rigid body. For the axisymmetric case with vertical translation, the coupled step reduces exactly to a small dense nonlinear problem for the film pressure, with the bulk eliminated through a $2x2$ affine map.
  The model is implemented in NGSolve and compared with the experiments of Hagemeier et al. (2021) and the Eulerian FSI simulations of Wahl et al. (2021a). For a PTFE ball the approach agrees with the Eulerian FSI to 1\%. For a soft rubber ball (St $\approx 120$) the purely elastic model gives about three times the measured rebound. Material damping is the most important missing effect: a Kelvin--Voigt compliance with loss factor $\tanδ=0.6$ gives 4.0\,mm, against 4.4\,mm measured. A planar version of the model is compared with the recently published 2D benchmark of Corti et al. (2026).
  The radius of the film patch is the only numerical parameter of the splitting. It is fixed by one a-priori rule for all configurations, derived from a dry Hertz estimate of the approach, and the results depend only weakly on it.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for strong normal shocks in kinetic relaxation models and the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for kinetic equations have mostly been applied near equilibrium and judged by density, velocity and temperature. Here a network trained on the kinetic equation alone, with no reference data in the loss, solves steady normal shock waves and is assessed in eight fields: density, velocity, temperature, heat flux, stress, a third-order moment and two fourth-order moments. The network corrects a mixture of the two end-state Maxwellians by an unbounded, signed factor with exact inflow; the loss, the residual in three norms with conservation terms, is minimised by Adam and a self-scaled quasi-Newton method with continuation in the Mach number. For the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation at Mach 8, in a comparison made once after reference-free tests, the largest relative $L^2$ difference from direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) over the eight fields is 0.19 per cent; at Mach 10 it is 0.34 per cent. The distribution function itself agrees with the reference over six decades in velocity space. For the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) model, a blind prediction at Mach 50 gives density, velocity and temperature to about 0.1 per cent and exposes a loss of accuracy confined to the two fourth-order moments. Its origin is identified as a passive reduced distribution that carries little weight in the loss; with a larger weight on that distribution and a longer optimisation, both moments are within 3.2 per cent of the discrete-velocity solution up to Mach 70 and 7.1 per cent at Mach 100. The Shakhov model is solved to Mach 20 and a Rykov-type model of nitrogen to Mach 15.

title: Cavitation inception delayed by structured surface roughness
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: Cavitation inception over structured rough surfaces is investigated experimentally in the diverging section of a Venturi. The diverging wall carries laser-etched checkerboards of square cavities with roughness aspect ratios $0.03 \leq k/d \leq 0.72$, tested at a Reynolds number of 95 160. Inception cavitation numbers were measured together with high-speed shadowgraphs of the near-wall flow, from which upstream-migrating nuclei were tracked and vapor-masked velocity fields were obtained by optical flow. Smooth walls recessed by the etched volume served as a control. The roughness delays inception, most strongly at intermediate $k/d$, where the inception cavitation number falls from 4.07 on the smooth wall to 3.33-3.46, whereas the recessed walls show no delay. The supply of nuclei is similar on all surfaces, so the delay does not come from a lack of nuclei. Instead, the roughness changes the near-wall flow. For $0.08 \leq k/d \leq 0.444$, a mean reverse-flow layer forms along the wall beneath a lifted shear layer, and vapor at inception appears further from the throat and away from the wall. At $k/d = 0.72$ the flow reverses only intermittently and the delay is smaller. On all surfaces except $k/d = 0.08$, the local cavitation number at inception varies linearly with the near-wall fluctuation energy, consistent with nuclei activated by pressure excursions about 6-8 times the r.m.s. fluctuation. The roughness thus delays inception not by limiting the nuclei, but by weakening the near-wall fluctuations that reach them.

title: Finite amplitude shape oscillations of magnetic microbubble under uniform magnetic field
summary: This study presents a theoretical model for the non-spherical oscillations of a lipid-encapsulated bubble infused with magnetic particles and subjected to a uniform magnetic field. Since the applied magnetic field is uniform, its gradient vanishes, making the existing weakly magnetic membrane theory inapplicable. To overcome this limitation, an alternative formulation that accounts for both the thinness and weak magnetic nature of the bubble shell is developed. Using this formulation, the induced magnetic field is calculated for a spherical bubble and incorporated into a Lagrangian framework for describing the non-spherical oscillations. The resulting governing equations for the radial and shape modes are then derived. The analysis shows that both the natural frequencies and exponential stability of the shape modes increase with increasing applied magnetic field. The frequency response of the shape modes shifts towards higher frequencies as the applied magnetic field is increased, consistent with the increase in their natural frequencies. Furthermore, finite-amplitude oscillations exhibit a period-doubling sequence and progressively transition towards chaotic behaviour with increasing magnetic field strength.

title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators
summary: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

title: Beyond the quasi-steady approximation: Modeling unsteady flows from steady solution families
summary: Many flow systems have well-established steady-state relations, but applying them quasi-steadily under unsteady forcing neglects memory effects. This study develops a modeling framework extending steady-state relations to unsteady flows by closing dynamic departures from the instantaneous steady state. Integral conservation laws determine the explicit balance structure, while finite-order temporal closures approximate unresolved spatial dynamics responsible for the memory effect. This formulation preserves the prescribed nonlinear steady-state relations as equilibria under constant forcing. Canonical benchmarks in laminar and turbulent channel flows and shallow-water wave propagation demonstrate that the required temporal structure depends on spatial memory and forcing timescale. First-order relaxation captures viscous diffusion, whereas wave propagation and boundary reflections require higher-order models for oscillatory memory. Modal analysis further reveals that the required dynamic resolution depends on the predicted quantity, with wall shear being more sensitive to higher viscous modes than bulk flow rate. Nonlinear extensions with state-dependent steady relations and dynamic coefficients reproduce transient lag, relaxation, and oscillations under slow-to-moderate forcing, including finite-amplitude regimes. However, rapid finite-amplitude waves expose the limits of locally linearized closures in capturing nonlinear phase dynamics. This framework compactly extends quasi-steady approximations while preserving exact steady-state consistency.

title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions
summary: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries demonstrate transformative potential for physiological assessment, identifying hemodynamic markers associated with disease progression, and optimizing treatment. Unfortunately, these models rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, limiting confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation. Herein, we present a novel uncertainty quantification-finite element framework that integrates computationally efficient techniques to characterize and propagate uncertainty through patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms, while uncertainty in blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate is represented through probability distributions. Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) enabled efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying variability in time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index. Fourth-order PCE emulators converged across all three patients, yielding analyses of 505 models per patient, with median coefficients of variation ranging from 0.15-0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54-0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28-0.38 for cross-flow index, highlighting greater relative uncertainty in multidirectional WSS metrics. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that time-averaged WSS variability was governed by the individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing <2% of total variance. In contrast, velocity waveform uncertainty dominated variability in the oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7-34.5% and 26.6-37.8% of total variance, respectively.

title: Self-arresting vortex rearrangements in pinned spinning-down superfluids
comment: 9 pages, 3 tables, 3 figures, 3 animations. To be submitted to PRL
summary: Superfluids, in a spinning-down container with pinning centres, exhibit sudden collective migration of quantized vortices. The onset, progress, and termination of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we show that: 1) the first exodus of vortices occurs when a sector of the vortex array, having a minimum opening angle, is vacated close to the wall; 2) driven by this exodus, the superfluid flow near the boundary continually decreases in strength and arrests the exit; and 3) the resultant depletion region has well-defined dimensions---governed primarily by the critical unpinning velocity, the container size, and the initial rotation rate---that limit the angular momentum transferred to the container. We conclude by discussing the relevance to pulsar glitches.

title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions
summary: Tensor train (TT) methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics simulations by exploiting low-rank structure in discretized fields and operators. While the superfast Fourier transform (SFFT) has enabled efficient TT-based spectral solvers for periodic problems, corresponding representations for non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored. We introduce the superfast cosine and sine transforms (SFCT and SFST), extending the TT spectral framework to homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. Building on a quantum-circuit construction of the discrete cosine and sine transforms, we derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove that their TT ranks are bounded by $6r_S$, independently of the discretization order, where $r_S$ is the rank of the SFFT at the prescribed accuracy. The measured ranks plateau near 32 for grid sizes up to $2^{26}$ points. For Rayleigh-Bénard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve relative to a preconditioned physical-space TT solver while maintaining comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves a 2-6-fold speedup and a 4-7-fold reduction in memory consumption compared with the existing TT-based approach. The results establish an efficient TT framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.

title: Impact of Taylor-Aris dispersion on chemical patterns in confined channel flows
summary: Chemical patterns form through non-linear interactions between different species. We study how confined channel flows affect pattern formation using the Brusselator as a paradigmatic activator-inhibitor model. An invariant-manifold method for slender channels reduces the advection-diffusion-reaction equation to one spatial dimension, with species transported at the mean flow velocity and molecular diffusivities replaced by the classical Taylor-Aris dispersion coefficients. We obtain the phase diagram as a function of the Péclet number (i.e., the relative strength of advection to diffusion), the channel slenderness, and the diffusivity ratio of the species. Our analytical results demonstrate that the classical Turing criterion can become inverted at large Péclet numbers and, thus, channel flow can trigger pattern formation even when the molecular diffusivities violate the classical Turing condition, and conversely destroy pre-existing patterns. Both predictions are confirmed by direct numerical simulations, which show advected stripe patterns, whose wavelength can be predicted by our reduced theory, as well as oscillatory dynamics. These findings highlight that hydrodynamic flows can modify chemical mixing and thereby profoundly affect pattern formation in channel geometries.

title: Saddle-focus to saddle transition of 4D heteroclinic orbits resembling oscillatory and regularized shock waves of some dissipative Boussinesq systems
summary: Oscillatory and regularized shock waves have long been studied to understand the formation and dynamics of undular bores in shallow waters, phenomena that typically arise from the interplay between dispersion, nonlinearity, and dissipation. In this work, we investigate and describe the nature and shape of traveling wave solutions that resemble oscillatory and regularized shock waves of some Boussinesq-type water wave models known as Bona--Smith systems in the presence of dissipation. The associated traveling wave equations are solutions of four-dimensional dynamical systems, leading to both computational challenges and rich structural behavior. In particular, to describe the properties of these traveling waves, we analyze heteroclinic orbits that connect two distinct equilibria, one of which undergoes a transition in the four-dimensional phase space from a saddle-focus to a saddle point as the dissipation parameter increases. This transition governs the nature of the wave profile, which evolves smoothly from an oscillatory shock wave to a regularized (non-oscillatory) shock wave. To compute such solutions, we introduce a finite-difference-based numerical method tailored for this class of problems.

title: Critical ocean physics on the edge of AMOC instability
summary: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is expected to weaken under global warming, but whether this signifies a transient response or a tipping transition remains unclear. Distinguishing between these cases requires a physical understanding of the boundary separating ocean states leading to AMOC recovery from those leading to collapse. In a global ocean model with 1° resolution, we compute an AMOC edge state -- an unstable saddle equilibrium that anchors this instability boundary. The edge state maintains weak overturning sourced by marginal deep water formation in the Nordic Seas. Analyzing the North Atlantic freshwater and heat balances that govern the edge state dynamics, we show that near the edge state, thermal and haline components of the surface buoyancy flux approximately compensate. Surface buoyancy loss (gain) coincides with AMOC recovery (collapse). Our findings support using the regional net surface buoyancy flux as an indicator for the onset of AMOC tipping.

title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
summary: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope combines shared multiscale pressure encoding, learned scale fusion and sensor-probability averaging, allowing measurement sets to change without retraining. Separate models evaluate unstart detection and new-onset prediction within a 0.5-s future interval. Seven Mach-2.9 runs, each with one annotated event, cover downstream throttling, throat regulation and splitter adjustment; three are held out with fixed weights and source-derived settings. Across three training seeds, full-sensor detection achieves run-wise mean window $F_1$ scores of 0.834--0.964. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces detection-score variation across sensor subsets in both splitter runs while retaining mean scores close to those of the full sets. Regional detection favors cowl and high-speed-channel measurements during splitter adjustment and compression-side measurements during downstream throttling, consistent with their respective pressure responses. Complete-record evaluation shows that configurations with comparable window scores can produce different alarm timing and persistence. These findings connect sensor count and regional coverage to pressure discrimination and sequential alarm behavior, providing experimental guidance for configuring inlet monitoring systems.

title: Integrated lasing and dual-band gain in neodymium-implanted silicon nitride
summary: Lasers at wavelengths near 1 micrometer are used in quantum technologies, precision metrology, and sensing. Rare-earth gain at these wavelengths in photonic integrated circuits can reduce the size and enable the scalable fabrication of these lasers. We fabricate neodymium-based integrated waveguide amplifiers and a ring laser using neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride. The photonic integrated circuits were fabricated on a 200 mm commercial wafer platform, and individual dies were implanted with neodymium ions. We show that the amplifiers provide gain in two bands around wavelengths of 920 nm and 1100 nm, and we show lasing in a ring resonator. This demonstrates that neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride is a suitable gain material for integrated lasers.

title: Recipe for near-unity efficient frequency conversion via transient molecular modulation
summary: Frequency transduction technologies are an essential element for interfacing devices operating at distinct spectral regions. Specifically, the conversion of weak signals between different wavelengths is a fundamental requirement of quantum networks, where conversion efficiency is critical for preserving the statistical properties of light. In this regard, molecular modulation in gas-filled hollow-core fibers offers a promising approach for highly-tunable linear frequency conversion of classical and quantum light. However, recent experimental studies in this subject have struggled to overcome a saturation in conversion efficiency to about 70%, which, although high, might impair the faithful transfer of quantum properties upon conversion. In this work, we discuss a route to surpass this limitation that identifies the key factors to consider for obtaining quantum efficiencies exceeding 99%. These results might pave the way to viable fiber-based quantum transduction schemes for next-generation quantum networks.

title: Heat Reduction in Erbium-Doped Microresonator
summary: We investigate anti-Stokes fluorescence in a 106-micrometer-diameter silica whispering-gallery-mode microresonator coated with erbium-doped sol-gel, assessing its potential for reduced optical heating. Near-infrared fluorescence spectra acquired under pulsed excitation near 1.55 micrometers exhibit a mean emitted photon energy above the pump photon energy. Measurements over a temperature range of 25 to 62 degrees Celsius show that the mean fluorescence photon energy increases with externally controlled temperature. The measured pump-wavelength dependence is consistent with an absorption-weighted spectral model, which predicts an optimum near 1562.65 nm for the investigated spectral figure of merit. Resonance-dependent emission patterns further motivate a dual-frequency pumping scheme using two higher-order whispering-gallery modes. Calculated time-averaged field profiles indicate that complementary modal distributions can provide more uniform excitation near the equator. These results characterize spectral conditions relevant to fluorescence-based heat reduction and suggest a route toward improved spatial pump coverage. Demonstrating net optical refrigeration requires additional measurements of absorbed pump power and an independent thermal readout.

title: AI-Assisted Topological High-Harmonic Spectroscopy for Characterizing Crystal Symmetries and Nonlinear Responses
summary: Structured light has emerged as a unique tool for probing nonlinear light-matter interactions. Particularly interesting is its interaction with anisotropic media, such as crystalline materials, whose anisotropic responses encode information about their electronic properties. Recently, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy was introduced as an all-optical approach to extract the anisotropic nonlinear response of graphene from harmonic spatial intensity profiles. Here, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy is combined with artificial intelligence (AI) to retrieve the anisotropic non-linear response and crystal symmetry of atomically thin materials. A convolutional neural network is trained and validated to learn the inverse mapping between harmonic far-field intensity profiles and the nonlinear response of materials exhibiting different rotational symmetries. Comparisons with microscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations demonstrate the accurate retrieval of distinct effective nonlinear responses in single-symmetry crystals, such as single-layer graphene and bilayer graphene with different stacking orders, and in crystals exhibiting multiple symmetry components, such as monolayer hexagonal boron nitride. Macroscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations assess the robustness and applicability limits of the technique. These results establish AI-assisted topological high-harmonic spectroscopy as a fast, contactless tool for characterizing nonlinear optical responses and crystal symmetries without phase-resolved measurements, opening prospects for applications to complex systems such as polycrystals and van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Nonreciprocal state-selective splitting of eigenstates at a polarization exceptional point
summary: Non-Hermitian photonic systems can be engineered to exhibit exceptional points (EPs), where eigenvalues and eigenstates coalesce. Although perturbations near EPs have mainly been characterized through eigenvalue splitting, the branch-resolved evolution of the coalesced eigenstates under a tunable reciprocity-breaking perturbation remains less systematically explored. Here, we show that tunable nonreciprocal coupling can produce state-selective splitting of the coalesced eigenstates near a second-order polarization EP. Using temporal coupled-mode theory, we find that the corresponding off-diagonal perturbation produces a triangular Hamiltonian in the circular-polarization basis. In the ideal limit, one eigenstate remains pinned to the EP state, whereas the other is continuously reoriented by the perturbation. In a realistic scattering system, residual reverse-polarization conversion weakly displaces the nominally pinned branch, resulting in quasi-pinning. We numerically demonstrate this mechanism in a reflective magneto-optical metasurface supporting a circular-polarization EP of the reflection matrix near 582 nm. Full-wave simulations show that a perpendicular magneto-optical bias leaves one reflection eigenstate close to the EP state while reversibly displacing the other on the Poincare sphere. This asymmetric eigenstate evolution manifests as a magnetically tunable circular-dichroic reflection response. Our results establish a nonreciprocal route to state-selective eigenstate control near polarization EPs.

title: A library-based approach for inverse reconstruction of cavity depth using angle-resolved cathodoluminescence
summary: In nanofabrication processes, accurate metrology is a crucial step for obtaining control over the required critical dimensions in a device. Traditionally, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is used to obtain high resolution measurements of the lateral dimension, but obtaining depth information on a thick sample is more complex. In this work, we use angle-resolved cathodoluminescence (AR-CL) spectroscopy to resolve this third dimension. Using 30 keV electrons in the SEM, CL is created at the bottom of a micrometer scale cavity milled in a gold surface. We show that reflections of the CL off the cavity sidewalls produce an interferogram which is a sensitive probe for the cavity geometry. The interferograms can be modelled using the finite-difference time-domain method, and we demonstrate that a neural network trained on a library of these simulated patterns can be used to reconstruct the cavity depth. This approach establishes a proof of concept for AR-CL based depth reconstruction within a prescribed geometry and could form a route towards advanced three-dimensional metrology of complex nanostructures.

title: Topological terahertz fields from tunable vectorial currents
summary: Future information processing calls for photonic architectures with greater capacity, intrinsic resilience to noise, and direct integration with quantum materials and devices. Topological light pulses have recently emerged as promising candidates to meet these demands, yet the complexity underlying their unique properties also makes them challenging to generate, tune, and fully resolve in space and time. Here, we generate and actively tune topological light fields through transient vectorial currents in an optoelectronic metasurface. Incident linear polarization steers the local direction of photocurrents in graphene via nanoplasmonic resonators with triangular symmetry, while a global winding pattern enables continuous tuning between compressional and circulating charge flows. Under ultrafast excitation, these currents radiate single-cycle terahertz toroidal pulses spanning electric- and magnetic-dominant modes with dynamically evolving skyrmion textures. Full spatiotemporal mapping and reconstruction provide a complete visualization of the toroidal structure of light, directly tracing the closed field surfaces while continuously tracking skyrmion number and helicity throughout a single cycle. These results connect two-dimensional vectorial currents to rich three-dimensional electromagnetic field structures, while establishing a versatile integrated platform for higher-dimensional photonic information processing and emerging material spectroscopies.

title: Witnessing Gaussian Coexistence and Correlation-Ellipse Tomography
summary: Gaussian light is specified by second-order field moments, yet their hidden correlation geometry can demand higher-order intensity measurements. We establish a measurement hierarchy for "Gaussian coexistence", i.e., the simultaneous presence of cross covariance and cross pseudocovariance. For two zero-mean Gaussian modes with circular marginals, all unperturbed intensity moments of second or third order are blind to coexistence. In contrast, a balanced fourth-order residual provides a necessary and sufficient witness. Their identities, however, remain fundamentally ambiguous: recovering the two correlation strengths does not reveal which belongs to the covariance and which to the pseudocovariance. Unexpectedly, adding thermal fluctuations resolves this ambiguity: an independent, correlated thermal probe selectively modifies the covariance while leaving the pseudocovariance unchanged, allowing the two correlation strengths to be individually identified. Moreover, a coherent reference in only one arm then makes their relative phase accessible through third-order intensity correlation. Together, these measurements reconstruct a correlation ellipse and its Poincaré-sphere coordinates, determining the relative channel strengths and the ellipse orientation. The framework separates what intensity detection can witness, what thermal probing can identify, and what a single phase reference can orient, turning inaccessible Gaussian correlation structure into a quantitatively reconstructible geometry.

title: Propagation-tunable fractional Stokes skyrmions in conical refraction
summary: Conical refraction in a biaxial crystal generates Stokes textures whose finite-domain skyrmion number takes fractional values tunable through free-space propagation, while the underlying azimuthal winding remains unchanged. For a circularly polarised Gaussian input, the skyrmion number is governed by the boundary Stokes parameter, $N_\mathrm{sk}=[1-s_3(R_\mathrm{cut},Z)]/2$. Six-state polarimetry reveals fractional values of 0.523, 0.565 and 0.266 in the Lloyd, Poggendorff and Raman regions, respectively, in close agreement with Belsky-Khapalyuk-Berry predictions of 0.530, 0.550 and 0.250, and reproduces the predicted longitudinal evolution. Conical refraction thus provides a passive route to propagation-tunable fractional Stokes skyrmions, in which continuously evolving polarisation geometry coexists with a fixed topological winding.

title: Dynamic tuning of anisotropy-induced quasi-bound-states-in-the-continuum in liquid-crystal integrated dielectric metasurfaces
summary: Symmetry-protected quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) in all-dielectric metasurfaces can be excited either by introducing a geometrical asymmetry into the unit cell or by illuminating the metasurface under oblique incidence. To date, tuning the coupling strength of such qBICs to the continuum has mainly relied on control of the geometrical asymmetry. Here, we show that qBICs can also be induced in a symmetric dielectric metasurface by embedding the latter into an anisotropic birefringent medium, and that they can be actively tuned by either rotating the anisotropy axis of the medium or by varying the degree of anisotropy. We experimentally implement a corresponding system by embedding a highly symmetric silicon nanocylinder metasurface into a nematic liquid crystal (LC) cell. Importantly, the LC does not only provide the desired birefringence, but also dynamic control of its strength as well as of the orientation of its anisotropy axis in response to different external stimuli. Specifically, applying voltage across the LC cell, where the LC molecules are pre-aligned along one of the lattice directions of the metasurface, enables out-of-plane rotation of the anisotropy axis of the LC medium. Meanwhile, its birefringence can be tuned by changing the temperature. In our experiments, the coupling of the qBICs to the radiation continuum is first maximized by the application of 25 V across the LC cell at room temperature. We then systematically tune the temperature and show that the resonance depth of the qBIC modes, which is associated with their coupling strength to the continuum, of the qBIC modes increases monotonously with birefringence. Our findings establish anisotropy-induced qBICs in LC integrated dielectric metasurfaces as a promising platform for actively reconfigurable metasurfaces and their applications in displays, optical modulation and tunable photonic devices.

title: Quantum Tautochrone for photons and atoms
summary: The tautochrone problem, in which the travel time to a common point is independent of the starting position, has served as a foundational model in classical mechanics. Here we establish its quantum counterpart in engineered photonic waveguide arrays and atomic optical lattices, where nonuniform couplings drive photons and particles launched from different positions to converge simultaneously at a common site. Using higher-order correlation functions, we show that this quantum tautochrone effect holds for both bosons and fermions, with quantum statistics governing the character of the convergence: bosons converge onto the same site, while fermions, constrained by Pauli exclusion, gather at neighboring sites. For bosonic atoms, we further show how the tautochrone dynamics is shaped by lattice inhomogeneity, phase-space structure, and on-site interactions.

title: Magnetometry and slow light in PT-symmetric cavity optomechanics
summary: The generation of optical higher-order sidebands, which produces new frequencies with regular spectral separation, holds significant promise for applications in optical communication and quantum metrology. We investigate second-order sideband generation and tunable slow-fast light effects in a parity-time (PT)-symmetric cavity optomechanics and propose an enhanced magnetometer scheme. We demonstrate that the PT-symmetric structure, an external magnetic field, and the photon tunneling strength provide powerful and flexible control over both the second-order sideband efficiency, as well as the broadening and switching of slow-fast light propagation. Operating in the PT-symmetry-protected phases, our magnetometer based on the second-order sideband achieves a theoretical sensitivity at the picotesla level, surpassing the performance of previous optomechanical approaches. Our results offer new strategies for magnetic field sensing and optical transmission control, paving the way toward applications in quantum sensing and optical information storage.

title: Tweezing microparticles by tightly focused optical skyrmionic fields
summary: The concept of skyrmions, once translated to the optical domain, provides a topological framework to investigate structured light-matter interactions. However, their practical use for the manipulation of material systems remains barely explored. Here, we experimentally demonstrate trapping and tunable orbital motion of dielectric microparticles in tightly focused skyrmionic polarization textures prepared using a compact spin-orbit optical element. We explore the tweezing capabilities at fixed topology either by varying the relative weights of the orthogonally polarized components or by switching between skyrmion and bimeron polarization textures. Vectorial focusing and optical-force calculations qualitatively reproduce the experimental observations. These results motivate extending skyrmionic light to the manipulation of micro-objects, including birefringent and chiral samples.

title: Competing Symmetry Breakings and Spontaneous Parity Restoration in Desynchronously Pumped Kerr Resonators
summary: Symmetry breaking is a cornerstone of nonlinear science, where stronger driving typically compounds parity loss across coupled degrees of freedom. Here, we uncover a counterintuitive symmetry-restoring transition driven by the competition between internal spontaneous polarization symmetry breaking (PSB) and external explicit temporal symmetry breaking (TSB) in desynchronously pumped Kerr resonators. Tuning pump-cavity desynchronization steers dissipative cavity solitons from pure PSB, through a robust hybrid symmetry-breaking (HSB) regime where both asymmetries coexist, into a pure TSB state accompanied by the abrupt, spontaneous restoration of polarization parity. Using collective-coordinate perturbation theory, we map the effective Ginzburg-Landau potential landscape and show that kinematic drift weakens local driving until a saddle-node bifurcation eliminates the temporal confining barrier. Corroborated by full Ikeda-map simulations across the phase boundary, our results demonstrate how driven-dissipative systems sacrifice internal order to satisfy external kinematic constraints, offering a general paradigm for competing order parameters in multidimensional nonlinear systems.

title: Temporal Soliton Waves in Modern Fiber Laser Systems
comment: This is the review article, which belongs to one of chapter for book: Handbook of Optical Fibers
summary:
This chapter provides a comprehensive survey of temporal soliton-wave
  in modern fiber systems. Temporal soliton waves constitute a broad class of nonlinear localized structures in modern fiber laser systems, arising from different balances among dispersion, nonlinearity, gain, loss,
  spectral filtering, and various forms of cavity coupling. We review the underlying theory, basic experimental findings, and practical methods for the generation, real-time characterization, and active control of soliton families, with a particular focus on recent progress reported for mode-locked fiber-laser platforms. The families covered in the chapter include dissipative solitons, soliton molecules (bound states), and dispersion-managed solitons. For each species, we focus on the pulse energy, duration, stationary and breathing states, and emerging intelligent (machine-learning-assisted) control strategies.

title: Mechanisms of turnkey soliton generation in self-injection-locked photonic-crystal ring resonators
summary: Turnkey generation of dissipative Kerr solitons in photonic-crystal ring resonators relies on the interplay between engineered mode splitting, self-injection locking, and modulation instability, yet the mechanism governing soliton initiation and number selection remains incompletely understood. We investigate this interplay using coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with a self-consistent nonlinear self-injection-locking condition. Analysis of continuous-wave steady states and their locking stability reveals operating points accessible through feedback-induced transitions between split resonances. Evaluating modulation-instability gain at these points identifies conditions for comb initiation and links the dominant unstable sideband modes to soliton-number selectivity. Direct time-domain simulations corroborate the analysis, showing that appropriately chosen mode splitting enables highly repeatable single-soliton generation without external laser-frequency scans. The final soliton number is nevertheless shaped by subsequent nonlinear evolution and feedback-induced detuning changes, rather than by the initial instability alone. We also show that larger dispersion suppresses higher-order unstable modes and favors lower soliton numbers.

title: Theory of modulation instability for coupled microresonators
summary: Thanks to hybridization phenomena, coupled microresonator systems enable modulation instability (MI) of the continuous wave background field across all possible dispersion combinations: anomalous-anomalous, normal-normal, and anomalous-normal microrings. Here, using the Lugiato-Lefever model in the supermode basis for two coupled microresonators with arbitrary second-order dispersion coefficients, arbitrary losses, and coupling strength, we derive a general eigenvalue problem for the $4\times 4$ matrix. We consider the regime of resonance splitting, in which the pump couples only to one of the two supermodes, allowing us to obtain analytical expressions for the stationary continuous-wave field distributed over the coupled system. When the microresonators have similar geometry, the antidiagonal elements of the eigenvalue-problem matrix nearly vanish, and we obtain a fully analytical solution for the MI gain rate for the entire range of coupled microresonator devices. Finally, we investigate cases in which the analytical treatment must be supplemented with more accurate numerical solutions of the MI eigenvalue problem, though even then the analytical theory captures the main features of the four-wave mixing process and the gain-rate behavior.

title: Phase matching of high-order harmonics driven by a combined coherent and bright squeezed vacuum field
summary: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) driven by non-classical light provides new insights into light-matter interactions and paves the way to quantum attosecond spectroscopy. Achieving phase matching is vital for generating bright HHG sources, while it has received comparatively limited attention in quantum-light-driven HHG. In this work, we investigate the phase matching of HHG driven by an intense coherent field combined with a weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) field, using a semiclassical ensemble of coherent-field realizations sampled from the Husimi-$Q$ probability distribution. We reveal the physical mechanism behind the distinct pressure dependence of the harmonic yields for odd, even and half-integer sidebands spectral components, as observed in our previous experiment [arXiv:2607.20941]. The simulations and phase-matching model demonstrate that the BSV-induced perturbation of the electron action phase could introduce an additional sub-cycle phase mismatch, such that the amplitude of sub-cycle bursts could be significantly modified by gas pressure after macroscopic propagation, even when the harmonic yield is near the optimum. The resulting amplitude asymmetry of sub-cycle bursts leads to a significant intensity contrast between half-integer sidebands harmonics, manifesting as distinct pressure dependence of their yields. Our findings reveal the phase-matching mechanism in two-color quantum-light-driven HHG, and suggest opportunities for macroscopic control of the non-classical HHG source.
